hints: Focus on what each halogen can and cannot do as an oxidising agent, and remember oxidising strength changes down Group 17.
Recall the silver nitrate test colours, white is for chloride while bromide gives a cream precipitate, and that gaining electrons makes an anion not a cation.
Put the displacement rule together, a halogen can only oxidise a halide below it, so check whether bromine is above or below chlorine.
walkthrough:
**Recall the silver nitrate test**

Think of this as an identification test for halides. The colour tells you which halide you have.

$$\text{Ag}^{+}(aq) + \text{X}^{-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{AgX}(s)$$

**Check the precipitate colours**

Chloride gives white $\text{AgCl}$, bromide gives cream $\text{AgBr}$, iodide gives yellow $\text{AgI}$. So a white precipitate means chloride, not bromide.

**Recall halogen oxidising strength**

Halogens act as oxidising agents by gaining electrons. Strength decreases down the group: $\text{F}_2 > \text{Cl}_2 > \text{Br}_2 > \text{I}_2$.

**Apply the displacement rule**

A more reactive halogen (higher up) will oxidise the halide ion of one below it, but not the other way round. Since bromine is below chlorine, this reaction does not happen:
$$\text{Br}_2 + 2\text{Cl}^{-} \rightarrow \text{no reaction}$$

**Check ions and reducing strength**

When fluorine gains an electron it forms a negative ion, an anion, not a cation:
$$\text{F} + e^{-} \rightarrow \text{F}^{-}$$
Reducing strength of halides increases down the group, so $\text{I}^{-} > \text{Br}^{-} > \text{Cl}^{-}$. Iodide is the strongest reducing agent.

options.A: Incorrect. Bromide ions give a cream precipitate of $\text{AgBr}$ with silver nitrate, not white. The white precipitate $\text{AgCl}$ is the test for chloride ions. This option confuses the two colours.
options.B: Correct. Chlorine is above bromine in Group 17, so $\text{Cl}_2$ is a stronger oxidising agent than $\text{Br}_2$. Bromine cannot take electrons from chloride ions, so no oxidation occurs when bromine is added to sodium chloride solution.
options.C: Incorrect. Accepting electrons always forms a negative ion, an anion. Fluorine reacts as $\text{F} + e^{-} \rightarrow \text{F}^{-}$. A cation is formed by losing electrons, which halogens do not do in this context.
options.D: Incorrect. Reducing strength of halide ions increases down the group because larger ions lose electrons more easily. Iodide is a much stronger reducing agent than chloride, so the order is reversed here.
